ga-static-hq.whatItIs: Fixed institutional facts: which city an institution is headquartered in, its tagline, founding year, and who currently heads it. Covers the 12 public sector banks, major private banks, every financial regulator, and the international bodies (WADA, NALSA, ASEAN, IMF) that IBPS drops into the same question slot.
ga-static-hq.coreMethod:
1. Build ONE table, five columns and nothing else: Institution | HQ city | Tagline | Year established | Current head. Fill roughly 45 rows: the 12 PSBs, the 8-10 largest private banks, the regulators and DFIs (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, EXIM Bank, DICGC, NPCI, IBA), and 15-20 international organisations.
2. Cluster the rows by CITY, never alphabetically by bank name. When the question asks 'which of these is headquartered in Chennai', you want to retrieve a city-group, not scan 12 banks one at a time. Your groups: Mumbai (the big one), Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, New Delhi, and a small 'odd cities' group.
3. Learn the ODD ONES first, because those are exactly what gets asked. Nobody asks where SBI is. They ask Central Bank of India (Mumbai), Indian Bank (Chennai), Indian Overseas Bank (Chennai), UCO Bank (Kolkata), Bank of Maharashtra (Pune), Punjab & Sind Bank (New Delhi), Bank of Baroda (Vadodara), Canara Bank (Bengaluru).
4. For taglines, store only the FIRST DISTINCTIVE WORD, not the whole sentence. The five options in the paper differ on that one word; the rest of the sentence is padding you never need to reproduce.
5. Keep current MD/CEO/Chairman names on a SEPARATE 'volatile' sheet that you rewrite monthly. Never write a person's name into the stable table — it rots and contaminates a table you otherwise never have to touch again.
6. Test only by REVERSE cue. Cover the HQ column and go bank-to-city; then cover the bank column and go city-to-banks; then tagline-to-bank. Reading the table top-to-bottom feels like studying and produces nothing.
7. Learn the 2019-20 amalgamation map as a separate four-line note (Dena + Vijaya into BoB; Corporation + Andhra into Union Bank; Syndicate into Canara; OBC + United Bank into PNB; Allahabad into Indian Bank). IBPS still uses the dead bank names as distractor options.
tricks: City-cluster retrieval: Chennai = Indian Bank + Indian Overseas Bank (both start with 'Indian', both Chennai — one hook, two answers). Kolkata = UCO Bank + Bandhan Bank. Bengaluru = Canara Bank. Pune = Bank of Maharashtra. Vadodara = Bank of Baroda. Everything else PSB is Mumbai or New Delhi. Six groups replaces twelve independent facts.

Tagline distinctive-word index: 'Banker to Every Indian' = SBI; 'India's International Bank' = BoB; 'Relationship Beyond Banking' = BoI; 'Good People to Bank With' = Union Bank; 'Good People to Grow With' = IOB; 'Together We Can' = Canara; 'The Name You Can Bank Upon' = PNB; 'Honours Your Trust' = UCO; 'Your Own Bank' = Indian Bank; 'One Family One Bank' = Bank of Maharashtra; 'Where Service is a Way of Life' = Punjab & Sind. Recall the distinctive word only — never the sentence.

The 12-PSB filter: after the mergers there are exactly twelve public sector banks. Any option naming a bank outside those twelve dies instantly on a 'which of the following is a public sector bank' question, and the merger map tells you which names are dead.

Only five establishment years actually get asked: 1806 (Bank of Calcutta, ancestor of SBI), 1894 (PNB, first bank run entirely by Indians), 1911 (Central Bank of India, first wholly Indian-owned and Indian-managed), 1935 (RBI), 1969 and 1980 (the two nationalisation rounds). Learn these six numbers and skip the rest.

Regulator HQ block learned as one line: SEBI Mumbai, NABARD Mumbai, EXIM Mumbai, DICGC Mumbai, RBI Mumbai — then only three exceptions to remember: IRDAI Hyderabad, SIDBI Lucknow, PFRDA and NHB New Delhi. Learning the Mumbai default plus three exceptions is faster than learning nine facts.

Geneva default for UN-family bodies: WHO, WTO, WIPO, ILO, ITU, UNCTAD are all Geneva. Learn 'Geneva unless told otherwise' and then memorise only the departures: UNESCO Paris, UNICEF and UN HQ New York, IMF and World Bank Washington DC, IAEA and OPEC Vienna, FAO Rome, ICAO Montreal, WADA Montreal, Interpol Lyon.
traps: Union Bank of India ('Good People to Bank With') versus Indian Overseas Bank ('Good People to Grow With'). IBPS knows this pair is confusable and puts both in the option set. Bank WITH = Union; GROW with = IOB (Overseas, grow outward).

Bank of Baroda's registered head office is VADODARA, not Mumbai. Its Baroda Corporate Centre is in Mumbai and half the internet says Mumbai. When both appear as options, the answer to 'headquarters' is Vadodara.
Options that split a city into two entries — 'Delhi' and 'New Delhi' listed separately, or 'Mumbai' and 'Navi Mumbai'. Read all five options before marking; the correct one is the precise form.
SIDBI (Lucknow) and IRDAI (Hyderabad) are the two most-missed regulator HQs in the whole section, precisely because every other financial regulator is in Mumbai or Delhi and aspirants pattern-match.

Revising MD/CEO names from a PDF more than two months old. Bank chiefs change constantly and a stale name is a guaranteed wrong answer, whereas HQ and tagline never change. If your source doesn't carry a date, do not trust its people-column.

Assuming an organisation's summit or event location is its headquarters. ASEAN is headquartered in Jakarta but its summit rotates among members every year — the paper asks both and they are different answers.
ga-static-hq.timeTarget: 10-12 seconds per question. These are the single fastest marks in the 200-mark paper — you either have the fact or you don't. If nothing surfaces in 10 seconds, flag it and move; no amount of extra time manufactures a headquarters.
ga-static-hq.masteryCheck: Blank sheet, six minutes, no lookups: you write all 12 public sector banks with the correct HQ city and tagline, and correctly place 15 of 20 major international organisations in their cities. You have mastered it when you can do this twice on different days with zero errors in the PSB half.

ga-static-cap.whatItIs: Place-to-place mapping. Country to capital to currency for the countries that appear in the news, plus the far more heavily asked Indian half: state capitals, and which state a national park, tiger reserve, lake, mountain, dam, GI-tagged product or festival belongs to. In IBPS papers this topic is the answer key for a large share of current-affairs questions, because those questions end with '...is located in which state?'
ga-static-cap.coreMethod:
1. Split into two registers and treat them completely differently. WORLD: country to capital to currency. INDIA: state to capital, and place-name to state.
2. For WORLD, do not learn 195 countries. Learn only India's neighbours, all SAARC and ASEAN members, the G20, and every country that appeared in your six-month current-affairs window. That is roughly 55 countries and covers around 95 percent of what is actually asked.
3. Learn currencies by FAMILY, never one at a time. Rupee family: India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Mauritius, Seychelles (and Indonesia's Rupiah). Dinar family: Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Serbia. Dollar family: USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Fiji, Brunei, Namibia. Riyal: Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Yemen, Oman — and Iran is Rial, spelt differently. Peso: Mexico, Philippines, Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Cuba, Uruguay. Then the singletons that actually get asked: Bhutan Ngultrum, Bangladesh Taka, Myanmar Kyat, Maldives Rufiyaa, Afghanistan Afghani, Thailand Baht, Malaysia Ringgit, Vietnam Dong, Cambodia Riel, Laos Kip, China Yuan, Japan Yen, both Koreas Won, Turkey Lira, Israel Shekel, South Africa Rand, Nigeria Naira, Ethiopia Birr, Kenya/Tanzania/Uganda Shilling, UAE/Morocco Dirham, Russia Ruble, Ukraine Hryvnia, Brazil Real, Peru Sol, Poland Zloty, Czechia Koruna, Hungary Forint, Sweden/Norway/Denmark/Iceland Krona or Krone, Switzerland Franc.
4. For INDIA, give every state ONE page in your folder that never moves. On it: capital, current CM, current Governor, two tiger reserves, one national park, one lake, one dam or river project, one festival, one GI tag, one stadium. The instant any news item mentions a place, the item goes onto that state's page. This is the mechanism that turns perishable current affairs into permanent static marks.
5. Drill the Northeast eight as a single ordered chant, because that block generates more questions and more errors than the rest of India combined.
6. Learn the small set of administrative facts that recur: three Union Territories have a Legislative Assembly (Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu & Kashmir); UTs have Lieutenant Governors or Administrators, not Governors; the states with a second seasonal capital (Himachal Pradesh — Shimla and Dharamshala; Maharashtra — Mumbai and Nagpur; Uttarakhand — Dehradun and Gairsain).
tricks: The Northeast alphabet trick, worth 1-2 marks every cycle: take the eight states in alphabetical order — Arunachal, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura — and their capitals fall in the fixed order Itanagar, Dispur, Imphal, Shillong, Aizawl, Kohima, Gangtok, Agartala. One ordered chant replaces eight independent facts and permanently separates the four that everyone confuses.

Continent-first currency elimination, usable even for a country you have never studied: African country implies Franc, Shilling or Dinar; Gulf country implies Riyal, Dirham or Dinar; Latin America implies Peso, Real or Sol; Southeast Asia implies Baht, Ringgit, Dong, Kyat, Riel or Kip. Three seconds of geography kills three of the five options before you have recalled anything.

GI-tag questions usually answer themselves because the product name contains the place: Pochampally is in Telangana, Bidriware comes from Bidar in Karnataka, Kanchipuram is Tamil Nadu, Banarasi is Uttar Pradesh, Madhubani is Bihar, Channapatna is Karnataka, Kolhapuri is Maharashtra, Feni is Goa. Keep a separate short list of only the GI tags whose name does NOT contain the place — those are the ones actually worth memorising.

Madhya Pradesh is the honest blind guess for tiger reserve and national park questions — it holds the largest cluster (Kanha, Bandhavgarh, Pench, Satpura). When you have no idea, MP is a genuinely better-than-random pick, which under a 5-option 0.25-negative scheme turns a break-even guess into a positive one.

Learn the parks whose state is counter-intuitive and skip the obvious ones: Betla is Jharkhand, Namdapha is Arunachal Pradesh, Simlipal is Odisha, Valmiki is Bihar, Dampa is Mizoram, Kamlang is Arunachal Pradesh. Everyone already knows Gir is Gujarat and Kaziranga is Assam; the paper asks the others.

Read the question for the word 'administrative', 'legislative' or 'commercial' before answering a capital question. Sri Lanka has Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte as legislative capital and Colombo as commercial; South Africa has three capitals. That single word decides the answer and takes two seconds to check.
traps: Assam's capital is DISPUR, not Guwahati. Dispur is a locality inside Guwahati, and IBPS routinely puts both in the options — this is one of the most-missed static questions in Indian banking exams.

The six lookalike national capitals: Switzerland is Bern (not Geneva or Zurich), Australia is Canberra (not Sydney), Canada is Ottawa (not Toronto), Brazil is Brasilia (not Rio), Turkey is Ankara (not Istanbul), USA is Washington DC (not New York). Every one of these has its famous city sitting in the option list as bait.
Myanmar's capital is Nay Pyi Taw, not Yangon. The change is old news but the wrong answer still appears in every option set.
Turkey's currency is Lira not Dinar; Israel's is Shekel not Dinar. Both countries sit in a region full of Dinars and the paper exploits the regional pattern-match.

The neighbours block is asked most and confused most: Bhutan Ngultrum, Nepal Nepalese Rupee, Bangladesh Taka, Myanmar Kyat, Maldives Rufiyaa, Sri Lanka Sri Lankan Rupee, Pakistan Pakistani Rupee, Afghanistan Afghani. Note that three of the eight are 'Rupee' variants — if you file them as a sub-family you stop guessing.
Confusing the state's largest city with its capital. It coincides for some states and not others, and the largest city is always in the options.

Answering a 'which state' question from the current-affairs half of your brain when it is really a static geography question. Mount Kamet, Pichola Lake and Kamlang Wildlife Sanctuary appeared as current-affairs-shaped questions but the answer is pure static geography.
ga-static-cap.timeTarget: 12-15 seconds per question. Capital and currency questions should be under 10 seconds; 'located in which state' questions get up to 15 because you may need one elimination pass.
ga-static-cap.masteryCheck: Five minutes, blank sheet, no lookups: all 8 Northeast states with correct capitals; all 8 of India's neighbours with capital AND currency; 15 tiger reserves or national parks placed in the correct state. Mastery means 100 percent on the Northeast and neighbour blocks, and at least 13 of 15 on the parks — repeated on a second day a week later.

ga-days.whatItIs: Fixed calendar observances — national and international — plus the specific theme announced for the current year and the organisation that declares or observes the day. The date half is permanently static; the theme half is fresh current affairs and behaves completely differently.
ga-days.coreMethod:
1. Build a twelve-row month sheet. For each month list only the 8-12 days that actually get asked, not the 40 that exist. Format: Date | Day name | Theme for this year | Declaring body or first-observed year.
2. Write each month's days IN ADVANCE, on the first of that month, from a month-wise list. Then read the news through the month — the news will confirm or correct the theme. Doing this retrospectively at the end of the year is how aspirants end up with 200 undifferentiated dates and no themes.
3. Learn themes for only the fifteen headline days. Themes are asked almost exclusively for: World Environment Day (5 June), International Yoga Day (21 June), International Women's Day (8 March), World Water Day (22 March), World Health Day (7 April), World Consumer Rights Day (15 March), World Telecommunication Day (17 May), World Population Day (11 July), International Literacy Day (8 September), World Tourism Day (27 September), International Day of Non-Violence (2 October), World Food Day (16 October), World AIDS Day (1 December), Human Rights Day (10 December), National Statistics Day (29 June). For every other day, the date alone is enough.
4. Learn the PERSON-ANCHORED days as a separate block, because the paper asks 'whose birth anniversary' as often as it asks the date: National Youth Day 12 January (Swami Vivekananda), National Girl Child Day 24 January, National Voters' Day 25 January, National Science Day 28 February (Raman Effect), National Technology Day 11 May (Pokhran-II), National Doctors' Day 1 July (B.C. Roy), Teachers' Day 5 September (Radhakrishnan), Engineers' Day 15 September (Visvesvaraya), National Unity Day 31 October (Sardar Patel), National Education Day 11 November (Maulana Azad), National Press Day 16 November, Children's Day 14 November (Nehru), Constitution Day 26 November (adoption of the Constitution, 1949), National Mathematics Day 22 December (Ramanujan), Kisan Diwas 23 December (Charan Singh), Good Governance Day 25 December (Vajpayee).
5. Drill in three directions in the same sitting: date to day, day to date, and day to person-or-theme. Single-direction revision fails because the paper picks the direction, not you.
tricks: The person-anchor is worth two marks for the price of one: knowing Vajpayee's birthday is 25 December hands you Good Governance Day; Ramanujan on 22 December hands you National Mathematics Day; Sardar Patel on 31 October hands you Rashtriya Ekta Diwas. Learn the person, get the day free, and the reverse question free too.

Check scope before you answer. Half the wrong options are the right date with the wrong scope — 'National' where the answer is 'International', or 'World' where the answer is 'National'. A two-second scope check on the stem eliminates two options.

Big-day questions come in two flavours and you must capture both: World Environment Day is asked for its THEME and for its HOST COUNTRY. Writing only the theme costs you half the possible questions from the single biggest day of the year.

'Which organisation observes this day' is a real and easy question form. Days are declared variously by the UN General Assembly, WHO, UNESCO, ILO, FAO, WMO or ITU. If the day is health-related the answer is WHO, education or culture is UNESCO, labour is ILO, food or agriculture is FAO, telecom is ITU. One categorisation rule answers the whole family.

If a date is given and you are blank, check whether it coincides with a famous person's birthday you happen to know — the paper's intended link is almost always the anniversary. This recovers marks you thought were lost.

Days that were renamed or moved in the last year are asked in that same year, without exception. When you see a 'renamed as' or 'date changed to' news item, mark it in red — it is the highest-probability item in this whole topic.
traps: Guessing a theme. Theme options are five plausible-sounding English phrases and elimination genuinely does not work on them. If the theme is not in your register, this is one of the very few GA questions where leaving it blank is correct — a blind 1-in-5 guess is exactly zero expected value.

Using a theme list published before the official announcement. Unofficial lists circulate months early with invented themes and they propagate across sites. For the fifteen headline days, confirm the theme against a second source or the declaring body's own page.
Revising days out of calendar order. Because you built the sheet month by month, revise month by month — mixing them destroys the calendar scaffold that makes recall work.

Confusing pairs on similar dates or similar names: World Health Day (7 April) versus World Health Organization Day; National Doctors' Day (1 July) versus other July observances; World Environment Day versus World Environment Health Day. Build the month sheet and these dissolve; keep a flat alphabetical list and they persist.
Assuming every 'International Day of ___' is UN-declared. Several are declared by specialised agencies, and 'declared by' is a distinct question.
Relying on last cycle's PDF. The date half never changes but the theme half changes every single year — never revise themes from a file older than the current calendar year.
ga-days.timeTarget: 10-12 seconds for a date-only question, 15 seconds for a theme question. If the theme is not in your register, skip in 5 seconds — do not stare at it.
ga-days.masteryCheck: Name any month and you can list 8 or more observances with exact dates in under 90 seconds. Separately, for all fifteen headline days you can state the current year's theme and the declaring body without hesitation. Verified on two different weeks, on months chosen at random rather than in sequence.

ga-awards.whatItIs: Who won what, in which field, given by which body — covering the recurring annual awards (Nobel, Booker, Padma, Jnanpith, Khel Ratna, Dadasaheb Phalke) and one-off honours conferred inside your six-month window. Roughly half the questions ask the FIELD or the AWARDING BODY rather than the winner, and that half is permanently static.
ga-awards.coreMethod:
1. Split into two buckets and treat them differently. Bucket A is CYCLIC awards whose category list is fixed and which recur every year. Bucket B is ONE-OFF honours — a foreign country's civilian honour conferred on an Indian, a UN award, a corporate or banking award.
2. Learn the AWARD-TO-FIELD map first, before any winner. This map is completely static and answers a large share of questions on its own, forever: Ustad Bismillah Khan Yuva Puraskar is performing arts for young artists; Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar is science and technology; Jnanpith, Vyas Samman, Saraswati Samman and Moortidevi are literature; Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna, Arjuna, Dronacharya and Dhyan Chand Award are sport; Dadasaheb Phalke is cinema; Sangeet Natak Akademi and Kalidas Samman are the performing and visual arts; Gandhi Peace Prize is peace and social work; Abel Prize is mathematics; Pritzker is architecture; Ramon Magsaysay is public service in Asia. One evening of work, and it pays every year in every bank exam you ever write.
3. For every actual award item, capture exactly five hooks and nothing more: Award name | Winner | Field | Given by (which body or ministry) | The distinguishing detail. That fifth hook — first woman, first Indian, youngest, posthumous, for which work — is asked about as often as the winner's name.
4. Revise by FIELD, not by date. Ask yourself 'who won in literature this window, in peace, in cinema, in sport, in science' — that retrieval shape matches the question's shape.
5. For the Nobels, memorise six categories and one keyword each for the reason. Never memorise the citation; one keyword survives exam pressure and a sentence does not.
6. For Padma awards, learn only Padma Vibhushan (usually a single-digit list) plus any Padma Shri that made headlines for being posthumous, unusual or viral. The full Padma Bhushan and Padma Shri lists are not asked at Clerk level and memorising them is a hundred wasted hours.
7. Keep a separate running line for Indians honoured by foreign governments — it recurs in every cycle.
tricks: Learn the award-to-field table to 100 percent before you learn a single winner. 'Award X is given in the field of ___' is asked every cycle, is completely static, and you can answer it correctly for the rest of your life without ever knowing this year's winner.

Star every item containing 'first', 'first woman', 'first Indian', 'youngest', 'oldest' or 'posthumous'. In this topic the superlative IS the question in roughly a third of items. Revise the starred items as a separate five-minute pass.

Field logic kills options in seconds: if the winner named in the stem is a Kannada writer, every science and sports award in the options is dead before you have recalled anything. Two or three eliminations from category alone turns a break-even guess into a clearly positive one.

Booker versus International Booker is itself a question: the Booker Prize is for a novel written in English; the International Booker is for a work translated into English, and the prize is SHARED between author and translator. 'Who translated it' is therefore a live question form.

Know the sporting-award hierarchy so you can pick the right tier: Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna is the highest sporting honour, Arjuna is for outstanding performance over years, Dronacharya is for coaches, Dhyan Chand Award is for lifetime contribution. The paper distinguishes these and so must you.

Do not skip banking and corporate awards (best bank, best digital bank, RBI-conferred awards, Euromoney and Asian Banker awards). They land in the Financial Awareness slot, which is where your competition is weakest.
traps: Confusing the award YEAR with the announcement year. Nobels are announced in October and conferred in December; Padma awards are announced on Republic Day eve and conferred months later. When a paper says 'Padma awards 2026' it means the list announced in January 2026.
Crediting the International Booker to the author alone. It is shared with the translator, and papers ask for the translator by name.

Recording the winner but not the work. 'Which book won the Booker' and 'who wrote it' are two separate questions generated from the same news item, and half the aspirants who captured one cannot answer the other.
Assuming Khel Ratna and Arjuna are interchangeable, or that the Khel Ratna is still named after Rajiv Gandhi. Name changes to awards are asked in the year they happen.
Studying the citation instead of the field. Nobody at Clerk level is asked to reproduce a Nobel citation; everybody is asked the field and the country.

Ignoring which MINISTRY confers a government award. Gandhi Peace Prize, National Film Awards, Khel Ratna and the Sahitya Akademi awards all have distinct conferring bodies, and 'conferred by which ministry' is a standard question.

ga-appointments.whatItIs: Who currently holds which post — across the RBI and financial regulators, the constitutional offices, the armed forces, the PSU banks, international organisations, and brand ambassadorships. Roughly a third of the questions are not about the person at all but about who appoints them, what the tenure is, or what the 'first-ever' tag was.
ga-appointments.coreMethod:
1. Work in three tiers, in this order, because this is the order they are asked. TIER 1 (about 35 posts, must be cold): RBI Governor and Deputy Governors, Finance Secretary, Cabinet Secretary, Chief Economic Advisor, CAG, Chief Justice of India, Attorney General, Solicitor General, Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners, UPSC Chairman, NITI Aayog Vice-Chairman and CEO, SEBI Chairman, IRDAI Chairman, PFRDA Chairman, NABARD Chairman, SIDBI CMD, NPCI MD, IBA Chairman, SBI Chairman, LIC Chairman, ISRO Chairman, DRDO Chairman, the three service chiefs, CDS, NSA, and the Home, Finance, Defence, External Affairs and Rural Development ministers. TIER 2: heads of international bodies — UN Secretary-General, IMF Managing Director, World Bank President, WTO Director-General, WHO Director-General, ADB President, AIIB President, NDB President, ICC and FIFA chiefs — plus newly elected heads of state of countries in the news. TIER 3: brand ambassadors of campaigns, state tourism boards, banks and sports bodies.
2. For each item capture six hooks: Person | Post | Organisation | Whom they replaced | Tenure or term length | First-ever tag. 'Whom did they replace' and 'what is the tenure' are both live question forms that most aspirants never record.
3. Keep the register as a LIVING single sheet. When a post changes hands, strike the old name on the same line and write the new one beside it. Never start a fresh list — you must be able to see the whole post list at once, because the question tests the current holder against the previous one.
4. Learn the WHO-APPOINTS-WHOM map as a separate, purely static block, because it is asked verbatim and never changes: the President appoints Governors of states, the CAG, the Chief Justice and other judges, the Attorney General, the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners, the UPSC Chairman and the Finance Commission chairman. The Chief Justice of India administers the oath of office to the President. The Chief Electoral Officer of a state is appointed by the Election Commission in consultation with the state government.
5. Learn TENURE LENGTHS in the same block, also purely static: CAG six years or age 65 whichever is earlier; CEC and ECs six years or age 65; UPSC Chairman six years or age 65; Supreme Court judges until 65; High Court judges until 62; RBI Governor three years, extendable; Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President.
6. Rotate the Tier 1 list once a week — five minutes, top to bottom, covering the name column. It takes almost no time and it is the difference between recalling four of five appointment questions and recalling one.
tricks: The who-appoints / who-administers-oath / what-tenure family is 100 percent static and generates 1-2 questions per paper across every bank exam. Learn it in one sitting, once, and it never needs relearning. This is the highest return-on-effort item in the entire GA syllabus.

Brand ambassadors are the cheapest sub-item in GA — one line each, no context needed, and at least one appears per paper (Incredible India, Viksit Bharat Buildathon, state tourism, bank campaigns, sports federations). Keep a running twenty-line list and re-read it in ninety seconds.

Organisation-type filtering: a career banker does not head ISRO, a bureaucrat does not head a sports federation, a judge does not head a bank. When you half-recognise a name, two options usually die on career category alone before you have recalled anything specific.

Write appointments as replacement CHAINS ('X replaced Y who replaced Z') rather than as isolated names. Revising the chain refreshes the previous holder for free, and 'whom did X replace' is a real question.
For international posts, always record the person's NATIONALITY. 'The newly appointed head of X is from which country?' is a standard variation and the nationality is easier to hold than the name.

When a question is date-anchored ('appointed in September 2026'), and the post changed twice in your window, the DATE decides the answer — not the most recent holder. Read the stem for a month before answering.
traps: Acting or interim appointment versus a full appointment, and 'appointed as' versus 'given additional charge'. IBPS uses both phrasings and the correct answer differs between them.
Confusing 'Chairman' with 'MD & CEO'. SBI has a Chairman; the other public sector banks have MD & CEOs. Picking the right person from the options requires the right title.
Not updating when a post changes a second time inside the six-month window. A living sheet fixes this; a date-wise diary does not, because you never see the two entries side by side.
Ignoring the 'first woman / first from state X / youngest / first non-IAS' tag. In about a third of appointment items, that tag IS the question.
Assuming Chief Ministers are asked more than Governors. Governors are reshuffled in batches, each reshuffle is news, and they are consequently asked more often than CMs.
Learning international heads only by organisation and not by name, then failing a 'who is the current Director-General of the WTO' question because you only recorded 'a Nigerian economist'.

ga-summits.whatItIs: International and domestic summits, ministerial conferences and expos held inside your six-month window — host city, edition number, theme, who represented India, and the headline outcome. It also carries a permanently static sub-part: the membership and member-count of every major grouping, which IBPS asks almost every cycle.
ga-summits.coreMethod:
1. For every summit item capture five hooks: Summit name and EDITION NUMBER | Host country and CITY | Theme | Who represented India | One headline outcome or declaration name. Host city and edition number are asked most, theme second.
2. Keep a permanent, separate table of the RECURRING groupings with their membership, current chair and next host: G20, G7, BRICS, SCO, QUAD, ASEAN, SAARC, BIMSTEC, IORA, NDB, AIIB, OPEC and OPEC+, the UNFCCC climate COP, the CBD biodiversity COP, WEF Davos, the IMF-World Bank annual meetings, the UN General Assembly session, and CHOGM. This table changes slowly and pays every year.
3. Learn the MEMBER-COUNT block as a single memorised strip, because 'how many members does X have' is one of the easiest marks in the paper and appeared verbatim in the last cycle: ASEAN 10, SAARC 8, BIMSTEC 7, QUAD 4, G7 7, EU 27, and G20 as 19 countries plus the European Union plus the African Union. Verify BRICS, SCO, NATO and OPEC counts against a current source each cycle, since those have changed recently.
4. For India-hosted events, record the CITY and the STATE, never just 'India'. The question is almost always 'held in which city' or 'held in which state'.
5. Record the 'next edition host' line for the big recurring summits — 'the next G20 Summit will be held in ___' is a standard question that you can answer months in advance.
6. Update the register AFTER the summit concludes, not when it is announced. Themes get finalised late and outcomes only exist at the end.
tricks: The chair rule: a grouping's annual summit is almost always hosted by the country holding the chairship or presidency that year. If you know this year's BRICS or SCO or ASEAN chair, you get the host country for free without having read a single summit report.

Edition-number arithmetic beats memorisation: if you know the summit is annual and you know any one edition-year pair, you can compute any other edition. Use it to sanity-check the options rather than storing thirty separate numbers.

Declarations are named after the host city, so city-to-declaration is automatic. If you know the summit was in a particular city, 'the ___ Declaration was adopted at which summit' answers itself in both directions.

Sort your summits into three buckets — India hosted, India attended, India absent. The third bucket is rarely asked; deprioritising it saves you a third of the reading in this topic with almost no mark loss.

'Who represented India' is a distinct question and the answer is NOT always the Prime Minister — the President, Vice-President, External Affairs Minister or Finance Minister attends many summits. Record the representative by name and designation every time.

When you cannot recall the host, use the theme's language or the summit's subject: a green-economy or climate summit in your window is likely in a Gulf or European city; a development or Global South summit is likely in Africa, Asia or Latin America. Rough, but it kills two options honestly.
traps: Confusing the summit's host with the organisation's headquarters. ASEAN is headquartered in Jakarta but its summit rotates among the ten members every year — the paper asks both.
Mixing the two COPs. The UNFCCC climate COP and the CBD biodiversity COP have completely separate edition numbering and separate hosts in the same calendar year, and IBPS uses both.
Recording the theme but not the edition number, or the edition number but not the theme, then meeting the other one in the paper. Both go on the same line, always.
Reading a pre-summit preview article and treating it as final. Announced, held and concluded are three different states, and outcomes only exist after the summit closes.
Assuming a summit's stated location is a country when the paper wants a city, or a city when the paper wants a state (for India-hosted events like India Maritime Week or the India Mobile Congress).
Letting the membership counts go stale. Groupings have expanded recently and an old member-count is a confidently wrong answer — the worst kind.

Separately and instantly, you can recite the exact membership count of ASEAN, SAARC, BIMSTEC, QUAD, G7, G20, BRICS, SCO and the EU, and name the current chair of BRICS, SCO and ASEAN.

ga-sports.whatItIs: Two very different things bundled under one heading. The permanently static half is trophy-to-sport mapping, which never changes and is asked every single cycle. The current half is tournament results, medal tallies, India's finishing rank, and individual records set inside your six-month window.
ga-sports.coreMethod:
1. Build three registers and work them in this order of yield. (A) TROPHY TO SPORT — static, build once, never rebuild. (B) TOURNAMENT RESULTS in your window. (C) RECORDS AND MILESTONES.
2. Build the trophy table by sport, once, completely. Cricket: Ranji, Duleep, Irani, Deodhar, Vijay Hazare, Syed Mushtaq Ali, Ashes, Border-Gavaskar. Hockey: Sultan Azlan Shah Cup, Sultan of Johor Cup, Agha Khan Cup, Beighton Cup, Rangaswamy Cup, Dhyan Chand Trophy. Football: Santosh Trophy, Durand Cup, Rovers Cup, Subroto Cup, Merdeka Cup. Badminton: Thomas Cup men, Uber Cup women, Sudirman Cup mixed. Tennis: Davis Cup men, Billie Jean King Cup women, plus the four Grand Slams and their surfaces. Table tennis: Swaythling Cup men, Corbillon Cup women. Chess, golf, polo, bridge and kabaddi trophies as a short tail.
3. For every tournament in your window, one line with seven fields: Event | Edition | Host city and country | Winner | Runner-up | India's position | Best Indian performer. 'India's rank' and 'whom did they beat in the final' are asked as often as 'who won'.
4. For every multi-sport event (Asian Games, Commonwealth Games, Olympics and Paralympics, World Championships, Asian Championships, Khelo India, National Games) record gold, silver, bronze, total AND India's overall rank. IBPS usually asks the total or the rank rather than the breakdown, but capture all four because you cannot predict which.
5. Record future hosts. 'The next edition of X will be hosted by ___' is a standard question that you can answer the moment the host is announced, often a year early.
6. Deliberately include para-sports. Para athletics, para badminton and para shooting results are asked at least once per paper and are skipped by most aspirants — this is free marks lying on the floor.
tricks: Learn trophy-to-sport to 100 percent. It is permanent, it is asked every single cycle in every banking exam, it costs one evening, and it is the closest thing to guaranteed marks in the whole GA syllabus.

The Asian royal-name cluster: Sultan Azlan Shah Cup, Sultan of Johor Cup, Agha Khan Cup are all HOCKEY. Merdeka Cup is the odd one out — football. Learning them as one block with one exception is far faster than four separate facts.

Fix one mnemonic, permanently, for the Thomas versus Uber pair — the single most-confused item in sports GK. Thomas is men's, Uber is women's badminton, Sudirman is mixed. Whatever device you choose, never change it.

Rank priors that honestly eliminate options: at a WORLD championship India usually finishes outside the top five but inside the top fifteen; at an ASIAN event India is usually third or fourth. When you do not know the exact rank, this kills the extreme options and turns a break-even guess into a positive one.
Nationality filtering on athlete questions: the name's origin usually eliminates two of the five country options immediately, even if you have never heard of the athlete.

Store records as 'holder plus the number', never as a narrative. The question is always 'who holds the record for X' or 'what is the record' — a sentence of context is dead weight under a 20-minute clock.

New leagues get asked in their first year, without fail. When a new franchise league launches (Indian Street Premier League and its equivalents), capture the sport, the launch year and the first champion immediately.
traps: Sultan Azlan Shah Cup versus Sultan of Johor Cup. Both are hockey, both are Malaysian, but Johor is the JUNIOR (under-21) tournament. When both appear in the options, read the stem for the word 'junior'.

Misreading which fact the question wants. Sports questions pack three facts into one sentence — host city, winning country and the beaten finalist — and this is the most commonly misread question type in the entire GA section. Read the stem twice; it costs three seconds and saves a mark.
Recording the winner but not the runner-up. 'X defeated whom in the final' is as common as 'who won'.
Filing Khel Ratna, Arjuna and Dronacharya announcements under sports. They are AWARDS news and belong in the awards register — but be ready for them under either heading in the paper.
Skipping para-sports entirely. Most aspirants do, which is exactly why the paper includes them.
Assuming the host city equals the winner's country. They coincide often enough that people stop checking, and the paper exploits that.

ga-defence.coreMethod:
1. Keep four registers. (A) EXERCISES: name | partner country or countries | host country | which service. (B) MISSILES: name | type | approximate range | developed by | test site. (C) SHIPS, SUBMARINES AND AIRCRAFT: name | class or project | builder | commissioned or launched | base or command. (D) ACQUISITIONS AND FIRSTS: what, with whom, deal value, indigenous content.
2. Learn the standing bilateral exercises as one block, because most of them recur annually and the map barely changes. USA: Yudh Abhyas (army), Vajra Prahar (special forces), Cope India (air), Tiger Triumph (tri-service amphibious). Russia: Indra. France: Shakti (army), Varuna (naval), Garuda (air). UK: Ajeya Warrior (army), Konkan (naval), Indradhanush (air), Cobra Warrior (air, UK-hosted). Japan: Dharma Guardian (army), JIMEX (naval), Veer Guardian (air). Australia: AUSTRAHIND (army), AUSINDEX (naval), Pitch Black (air, Australia-hosted). Neighbours: Surya Kiran (Nepal), Mitra Shakti and SLINEX (Sri Lanka), Sampriti and Bongosagar (Bangladesh), Ekuverin (Maldives). Central Asia and Gulf: Dustlik (Uzbekistan), Khanjar (Kyrgyzstan), Al-Nagah and Eastern Bridge (Oman), Desert Cyclone and Zayed Talwar (UAE). Multilateral: Malabar (India, USA, Japan, Australia — naval), Milan (India-hosted, multinational naval), Bright Star (EGYPT-hosted, multinational).
3. Learn missiles by FAMILY rather than individually: Agni (surface-to-surface ballistic, range scales with the number), Prithvi (short-range ballistic), BrahMos (supersonic cruise, India-Russia joint venture), Akash and QRSAM and VSHORADS (surface-to-air), Nag, Helina and MPATGM (anti-tank), Astra (air-to-air beyond visual range), Rudram (anti-radiation), Nirbhay and ITCM (subsonic cruise), Pinaka (multi-barrel rocket), Barak-8 (India-Israel), the K-series (submarine-launched), Pralay and Agni-Prime.
4. For ships, always record the CLASS and the BUILDER, not just the name. Project 15B destroyers and Project 75 Scorpene submarines are built at Mazagon Dock, Project 17A frigates at Mazagon Dock and GRSE, and INS Vikrant at Cochin Shipyard. 'Built by which shipyard' is a live question.
5. When an exercise appears, immediately ask three separate questions of yourself and record all three answers: who is the partner, which country is HOSTING this edition, and which service is involved. These are three different questions IBPS asks from the same news item, and hosting alternates for many bilateral exercises.
tricks: The language of the exercise name tells you the partner region and eliminates options in three seconds. Sanskrit or Hindi names (Yudh Abhyas, Vajra Prahar, Surya Kiran, Mitra Shakti, Sampriti, Ajeya Warrior) are India-bilateral. Arabic-derived names (Al-Nagah, Zayed Talwar, Desert Cyclone) point to Gulf partners. Central Asian names (Dustlik, Khanjar) point to Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. Animal or colour names (Nomadic Elephant for Mongolia, Pitch Black for Australia) are their own small block.

India's own single-service exercises never have a foreign partner: TROPEX, AMPHEX, Vayu Shakti, Gagan Shakti, Trishakti Prahar. If the question names one of these and the options are all foreign countries, the framing has changed — re-read the stem, because it is asking something else (which service, or where it was held in India).

Missile range banding lets you eliminate without exact figures: Prithvi sits in the short 150-350 km band, BrahMos in the roughly 300-800 km band, Nirbhay around 1000 km, and the Agni series scales upward with its number. Even without the precise figure, the wildly wrong options die.

Every commissioned Indian warship is based at one of four commands and the command names the port: Western is Mumbai and Karwar, Eastern is Visakhapatnam, Southern is Kochi, and the Andaman & Nicobar Command is Port Blair. Four options, and the command tells you which.
Record the DEAL VALUE for every acquisition. 'The deal signed with X was worth how much' is a standard question form, and the figure is easier to hold than the equipment specification.

When you cannot place an exercise, ask whether it is bilateral or multinational. Multinational exercises where India is only a participant (Bright Star, Pitch Black, Cobra Warrior, RIMPAC) are asked precisely because aspirants reflexively assume every exercise is India-plus-one.
traps: Bright Star is hosted by EGYPT and is multinational — India merely participates. This exact question appeared in the last cycle, and the trap is that aspirants read any exercise name as an India-bilateral.
BrahMos is India-RUSSIA; Barak-8 is India-ISRAEL. Swapping these two partners is the classic missile trap and it appears repeatedly.
'Launched' versus 'commissioned' for warships. These are different events on different dates, IBPS uses both words deliberately, and the answer differs.

Assuming DRDO develops and builds everything. DRDO develops, but Bharat Dynamics Limited produces missiles, Hindustan Aeronautics builds aircraft, Bharat Electronics builds electronics, and the shipyards build ships. 'Developed by' and 'manufactured by' are different questions.
Confusing Agni-V with Agni-Prime, or the submarine-launched K-series with the land-based Agni series. When the paper specifies the variant, the variant is the whole question.
Malabar's participant list expanded over time. Check the participant list for the specific edition the question names rather than answering from a general memory of the exercise.
Assuming the host of a bilateral exercise is fixed. Most India-bilateral exercises alternate between the two countries year on year, so 'held in which country' depends on the edition.
ga-defence.timeTarget: 15 seconds per question. Exercise-to-partner questions should be 10 seconds once the block is learned; missile and ship detail questions take the full 15.
ga-defence.masteryCheck: Given 30 exercise names on a blank sheet you write the correct partner country and the correct service for at least 27. Separately, for every missile tested inside your six-month window you state its type, its developing agency and its approximate range band without looking, and for every ship commissioned you name the builder.

ga-scitech.whatItIs: ISRO and space missions, Indian technology launches and indigenous platforms, national technology missions with their outlays, and health and biotech news. The recurring question shapes are 'which launch vehicle', 'developed by which company or agency', 'in which year', and 'what does this acronym stand for'.
ga-scitech.coreMethod:
1. Four buckets. (A) ISRO AND SPACE. (B) OTHER AGENCIES' SPACE NEWS that made headlines. (C) INDIAN TECH LAUNCHES — indigenous apps and platforms, semiconductor fabs, supercomputers, AI and quantum missions, 5G and 6G, drones. (D) HEALTH AND BIOTECH — vaccines, drug approvals, outbreaks, WHO declarations, medical firsts.
2. For every space mission capture six hooks: Mission name | Launch vehicle and variant | Launch site | Target or orbit | Number of satellites or payloads carried | The 'first ever' tag. The launch vehicle and the 'first' tag are asked most.
3. Learn the STATIC space table once and it never needs relearning: ISRO headquarters Bengaluru; VSSC Thiruvananthapuram; SDSC-SHAR Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh; URSC Bengaluru; SAC Ahmedabad; NRSC Hyderabad; IN-SPACe Ahmedabad; NSIL Bengaluru as ISRO's commercial arm. Plus the historical firsts, which are asked as often as current missions: Aryabhata 1975 as India's first satellite, Chandrayaan-1 in 2008, Mangalyaan in 2013, Chandrayaan-2 in 2019, Chandrayaan-3 and Aditya-L1 in 2023, and Gaganyaan as the crewed programme.
4. For national technology missions (National Quantum Mission, IndiaAI Mission, National Supercomputing Mission, Semicon India, National Green Hydrogen Mission), capture four fields: launch year | nodal ministry | outlay in crore | duration. The OUTLAY figure is asked more often than the mission's purpose.
5. For apps and platforms, always capture WHO BUILT IT. 'The Arattai messaging app was developed by which company' is exactly the question form, and Indian-company-builds-Indian-platform items are near-certain questions.
6. Keep a running ACRONYM column. A large share of sci-tech questions reduce to expanding an acronym — NISAR, IN-SPACe, NSIL, INSAT, GSAT, NavIC, RISAT, EOS, GAGAN, SSLV, LVM3. Each expansion is a five-second mark.
tricks: Launch-vehicle inference from payload type, which eliminates three options without recalling the mission: small satellites go on SSLV; earth-observation and polar sun-synchronous payloads go on PSLV; communication satellites to geostationary transfer orbit go on GSLV; the heaviest payloads, lunar missions and the crewed programme go on LVM3.

Every ISRO launch lifts off from Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh, so 'launched from which state' is a free mark. Learn the single exception — the new SSLV launch complex at Kulasekarapattinam in Tamil Nadu — and this whole question family is solved.

Star every item containing 'India's first', 'world's first' or 'indigenously developed for the first time'. In sci-tech, the superlative is what makes the item newsworthy and is therefore what makes it examinable.

The Indian-company shortlist is short enough to recognise on sight: Zoho, TCS, Infosys, Reliance Jio, Tata, L&T, HAL, BEL, BDL, Bharat Biotech, Serum Institute, Ola, Ather, Adani. When a question asks 'developed by which company' and the options mix Indian and foreign names, the Indian-launch context usually kills the foreign options immediately.
Record the ₹ crore outlay for every mission. Aspirants remember what a mission does and forget what it costs — and the cost is what gets asked.
For health items, record the APPROVING BODY along with the approval: WHO prequalification, DCGI approval and emergency use authorisation are three different things and the paper distinguishes them.
traps: Confusing Chandrayaan-2 with Chandrayaan-3 — their years, their outcomes (Chandrayaan-2's lander failed while its orbiter continued working; Chandrayaan-3 achieved the soft landing) and the landing site name. This pair is asked constantly.
Ignoring the launch-vehicle VARIANT when the question specifies one. PSLV-XL, PSLV-DL and PSLV-CA are different configurations and the paper does name them.
Treating a joint mission as pure ISRO. 'In collaboration with which agency' is a distinct question — NISAR is ISRO with NASA, and several missions have foreign partners.

Reading an ANNOUNCEMENT as a LAUNCH. Announced, approved by Cabinet, launched, and declared successful are four different dates from the same mission, and the paper is specific about which one it wants.
Skipping the outlay and duration figures for national missions because they feel like dry detail. They are the most-asked fields in that sub-bucket.
Confusing a disease's name with its pathogen's name in health items, and confusing 'declared a public health emergency' with 'outbreak reported'.
ga-scitech.timeTarget: 15 seconds per question. Acronym-expansion questions should be 5-8 seconds; mission-detail questions take the full 15.
ga-scitech.masteryCheck: For every ISRO launch inside your six-month register you state the mission, the launch vehicle, the launch site and the headline 'first' without looking. Separately, you expand 25 space and technology acronyms correctly in under three minutes, and you state the nodal ministry and outlay for five national technology missions.
questionPatterns: Chandrayaan-1 was launched in which year?
The Arattai messaging app was developed by which company?

The National Quantum Mission comes under which ministry and has an outlay of how much?
NISAR is a joint mission of ISRO and which agency?

ga-books.whatItIs: Two small, cheap, reliably-asked streams bundled together. Books: title, author, and the hook that made it news. Obituaries: the person, and above all the FIELD they worked in — because 'the late X was associated with which field' is the dominant question form.
ga-books.coreMethod:
1. Keep two one-line registers and never merge them. BOOKS: Title | Author | Genre in one word | The hook — is it an autobiography, a biography of whom, posthumous, translated by whom, released by whom, or the author's nth book. OBITUARIES: Name | FIELD IN CAPITALS | The single achievement they were known for | Any title or award they held.
2. Capture only books that meet one of four filters: written by or about a public figure, won an award, released by the President, Prime Minister, a minister or a Governor, or is an autobiography. General publishing news is never asked — ignore it entirely and save the reading time.
3. Write the FIELD FIRST on every obituary line, in capitals, before the name. The question gives you the name and asks the field, or gives the field and asks the name — and the field is the shorter, more retrievable half.
4. Revise author-to-book AND book-to-author in the same sitting, every time. This is the only defence against the option-swap trap, which is the entire game in this topic.
5. For translated works, record the ORIGINAL LANGUAGE and the TRANSLATOR. 'Translated from which language' is a standard question, and translation news items have become more frequent since Indian-language works started winning international prizes.
6. Record the ORDINAL when the news gives one — 'his fourth book', 'her second novel'. Papers ask the ordinal directly.
tricks: The first-person test resolves a whole class of questions in two seconds: if the title uses 'My', 'I', or a clearly first-person voice, it is an autobiography and the author IS the subject. If the title is about a person in the third person, it is a biography and the author is someone else.

'Released by whom' is a nearly free mark if you captured it, because the releaser is almost always the President, the Prime Minister, the Home Minister or a Governor — a four-way choice you can often reason to.

On obituary questions you can answer even having forgotten the name. The paper gives five names and asks the field, or gives the field and asks among five names — and field-clustering your obituary register (cinema, literature, sport, politics, science, music, business) means you retrieve by category rather than by name.
Titles containing a place name, an era or a person's name are usually literal about their subject — use that to eliminate two options when the question asks what a book is about.

Obituaries take twenty seconds each to learn and appear in nearly every paper. This is the single best effort-to-mark ratio in the entire GA section, and it is the item most commonly skipped as 'not important'.
When two authors in your window wrote books on similar subjects, write them on ADJACENT lines with a warning mark. Pre-empting the swap is far more effective than trying to untangle it in the hall.
traps: Author-swap. IBPS routinely places two authors from the same six-month window into the same option set, precisely because aspirants learn book-to-author in one direction only. Two-directional revision is the only fix.
Confusing the author of a biography with its subject. 'Who wrote the book about X' and 'who is the book about' are two different questions.
Skipping obituaries as low-value. They appear nearly every paper and cost almost nothing to learn.
Missing the 'posthumously released' or 'posthumously awarded' tag, which is sometimes the entire question.
Recording the book but not the ordinal when the news specified one, then meeting 'his fourth book is titled ___' in the paper.

Trying to eliminate options on a book question you did not capture. Unlike most GA topics, book-and-author options give you almost no category leverage — all five will be plausible Indian names. If it is not in your register, skip it fast.
ga-books.timeTarget: 12-15 seconds per question. Do not linger — this is one of the few GA topics where elimination genuinely does not work, so it is either an instant recall or an instant skip.
ga-books.masteryCheck: From your six-month register you go both directions: given 20 titles you name the author for at least 18; given 20 authors you name the title for at least 18. Separately, for every obituary in the register you state the person's field instantly, without needing to recall their biography.

ga-ranks.whatItIs: Global and domestic indexes and reports — India's rank, the total number of countries surveyed, who topped it, and above all which organisation PUBLISHES it. The publisher half is semi-static and reusable for years; the rank half expires every cycle.
ga-ranks.coreMethod:
1. One master table, four columns: Index or report name | Publishing organisation | India's rank and the edition year | Total countries surveyed and the topper.
2. Learn the REPORT-TO-PUBLISHER map first, because it is semi-static and because publisher questions outnumber rank questions at Clerk level. Human Development Index — UNDP. World Happiness Report — UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network. Global Hunger Index — Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe. Corruption Perceptions Index — Transparency International. Global Innovation Index — WIPO. Global Competitiveness Report, Global Risks Report and Global Gender Gap Report — World Economic Forum. World Economic Outlook and Global Financial Stability Report — IMF. World Investment Report — UNCTAD. State of World Population — UNFPA. State of the World's Children — UNICEF. Global Peace Index and Global Terrorism Index — Institute for Economics and Peace. Environmental Performance Index — Yale and Columbia. Henley Passport Index — Henley & Partners. World Press Freedom Index — Reporters Without Borders. Logistics Performance Index — World Bank. SDG India Index and the Multidimensional Poverty Index for India — NITI Aayog. Periodic Labour Force Survey — NSO under MoSPI. Economic Survey — Ministry of Finance.
3. Keep the RBI's own publications as a distinct sub-block, because they land in the Financial Awareness slot where your competition is weakest: Financial Stability Report (half-yearly), Monetary Policy Report, Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India (annual), RBI Annual Report, Consumer Confidence Survey, Bank Lending Survey, and the Report on Currency and Finance. 'Which report is published by RBI' and 'how many times a year is the Financial Stability Report released' are both live questions.
4. Always record the EDITION YEAR beside the rank. An index without its year is worse than useless, because it will confidently produce last year's answer.
5. Record whether India IMPROVED or DECLINED and by how many places. 'India improved by n places in the ___ Index' is a distinct question form.
6. Do not memorise the ranks of any country other than India, the topper, and occasionally India's immediate neighbours. Everything else is noise.
tricks: Learn publishers before ranks. Even when you have forgotten India's exact position, 'which organisation releases the Global Innovation Index' is a separate question you can still answer — and it is asked more often at Clerk level than the rank itself.

Naming-convention heuristic that eliminates two options: a 'Global ___ Index' is usually a non-UN think tank or specialist body, while a 'World ___ Report' is usually UN-family or the World Economic Forum. Rough, but it works often enough to be worth three seconds.

When India's rank is unknown, use the honest prior: India tends to sit mid-table on economic and innovation indexes and lower on press-freedom, hunger and gender-gap style indexes. That kills the extreme options at both ends and turns a break-even guess into a positive one.

Note the TOTAL number of countries surveyed for each index. That figure is stable year to year, is asked directly ('India ranked X out of how many countries'), and is much easier to hold than the rank.

Prioritise domestically-released reports — Economic Survey, PLFS, NFHS, SDG India Index, RBI's publications. They are asked more predictably than obscure foreign indexes and they double as Financial Awareness marks.

Learn the pairs that exist to confuse you as PAIRS, side by side: Human Development Index versus Human Capital Index, World Happiness Report versus anything WEF, Economic Survey versus Union Budget, RBI Annual Report versus Financial Stability Report.
traps: Attributing the Global Hunger Index to the United Nations. It is published by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe, and India routinely disputes its methodology — which is exactly why it is newsworthy and exactly why it is asked.
Confusing the Human Development Index (UNDP) with the Human Capital Index (World Bank). Different publishers, different indexes, both plausible-sounding.
Using last year's rank because your register did not record the edition year. Indexes are annual and a rank without a year is a coin flip.
Confusing the Economic Survey (Ministry of Finance, tabled just before the Union Budget) with the Budget itself, and confusing the RBI Annual Report with the Financial Stability Report.
Ignoring 'released by which ministry' for domestic reports. That is a distinct and easy question you will miss if you only recorded the number.
Recording the rank but not the topper. 'Which country topped the ___ Index' is asked about as often as India's own rank.
ga-ranks.timeTarget: 15 seconds per question. Publisher questions should be 8-10 seconds — pure table lookup.
ga-ranks.masteryCheck: You name the publishing organisation for 25 named indexes and reports without hesitation and with zero errors. Separately, for the roughly ten indexes released inside your six-month window you state India's rank, the total number of countries and the topper — with the edition year attached to each.

ga-agreements.whatItIs: Two streams: government-level bilateral and multilateral agreements between India and other countries, and institutional MoUs — most importantly bank MoUs, which are the highest-yield sub-item for a banking exam. The load-bearing fact is almost always the PURPOSE, not the date.
ga-agreements.coreMethod:
1. Two sub-registers. (A) BILATERAL AND INTERNATIONAL: India plus partner | sector | signed at which visit or summit | one headline number such as investment value or tenure. (B) INSTITUTIONAL MoUs: Party 1 (usually a bank, PSU or ministry) | Party 2 | purpose in five words maximum.
2. For bank MoUs the question is always 'Bank X signed an MoU with Y for what purpose', so write the PURPOSE in five words and no more: 'for co-lending to MSMEs', 'for the defence salary package', 'for agri-loan distribution', 'for EV financing', 'for the disbursement of state scheme benefits'. A paragraph of context is dead weight.
3. Revise by SECTOR, not by date. Defence agreements, energy and renewables, digital payments, trade agreements, health, education, space. Sector-clustered retrieval matches how the question is framed and is the only way this topic becomes revisable.
4. Keep a dedicated running line for UPI AND RuPAY INTERNATIONALISATION — which countries have begun accepting UPI, which have linked their domestic fast-payment systems with India's. This appears in nearly every banking GA paper and is entirely predictable.
5. Keep a separate line for TRADE AGREEMENT ACRONYMS and their partners: CEPA, CECA, ECTA, TEPA, FTA. The acronym-to-partner map is asked directly, and so is the full-form expansion.
6. Learn agreements in VISIT CLUSTERS. Agreements bunch around a head-of-state visit — five or six MoUs signed on the same day. Learning the cluster ('during the PM's visit to X, agreements on defence, energy, digital payments and skills were signed') is far more efficient than learning six isolated items.
tricks: Counterparty type tells you the purpose. An MoU with the Indian Army is a salary-package deal; with NABARD it is agricultural or rural credit; with a state government it is scheme disbursement; with an insurer it is bancassurance; with a fintech it is digital lending or payments. Recognising the counterparty answers the 'for what purpose' question without recalling the item.
Expand every acronym in your window. In this topic the full form is frequently the entire question — 'what does the C in CEPA stand for' is a real and easy mark.

Sector-plus-partner elimination: if you remember only that an MoU concerned renewable energy, the partner is very likely one of the small set of countries India does energy diplomacy with, and two or three options die on plausibility alone.
Record the NUMBER. 'An MoU worth $X billion' and 'a five-year agreement renewable for three' — the figure and the duration are asked, and they are easier to hold than the agreement's text.
The visit-cluster trick doubles as a memory aid for the state visits themselves, which are separately asked ('the PM visited which country in October 2026').

Bank MoUs almost always pair one large bank with one of five counterparty types: a fintech, an insurer, an armed service, a state government, or an agri or MSME body. Knowing the five types narrows the options before you have recalled anything.
traps: MoU signed versus agreement ratified versus deal operationalised. These are different stages on different dates and IBPS uses the exact word from the notification.
Getting the two parties the right way round. When both parties are banks or both are institutions, the paper swaps them in the options — capture both names, in order.

Assuming every 'India and X' agreement is government-to-government. Many are institution-to-institution: ISRO with a foreign space agency, SEBI with a foreign regulator, RBI with a foreign central bank. 'Signed between which two bodies' is a distinct question.
Ignoring the monetary value or the validity period because they feel like detail. They are precisely what is asked.
Filing agreements by date. This topic is unrevisable in date order — the question is framed by sector and partner, so the register must be too.
Missing bank MoUs entirely because they feel like corporate trivia. They carry double weight in a banking exam, counting under both current affairs and financial awareness.

ga-state.whatItIs: Everything that happened in a particular Indian state — schemes launched, 'India's first' facilities inaugurated, projects commissioned, festivals, and changes of Chief Minister or Governor. The dominant question form is 'X was launched in which state', which means this topic and static geography are functionally the same topic.
ga-state.coreMethod:
1. Give every one of the 28 states and 8 Union Territories ONE page in your folder that never moves. On that page: capital, current CM, current Governor or Lieutenant Governor, state animal and bird, major festivals, dances, and then two running columns — SCHEMES and INDIA'S FIRSTS.
2. The moment any news item names a place, write it onto that state's page the SAME DAY. This is the single most important habit in this topic. State current affairs kept in date order is unrevisable, because the paper asks it state-wise and never date-wise.
3. Give every state page an 'INDIA'S FIRSTS' column at the top. 'India's first ___ was launched in which state' is the most-asked form, and having a dedicated column means you revise exactly the right thing in ninety seconds.
4. For every state scheme capture four fields: scheme name | state | beneficiary group | benefit amount in rupees. The ₹ figure per beneficiary is asked as often as the state.
5. For 'X is located in which state' items — parks, dams, airports, ports, solar and wind projects, industrial corridors, temples, stadiums, GI tags — write them onto the state page even though they feel static. This is where the current and static halves fuse, and treating them separately is why aspirants miss both.
6. Maintain the 36-row CM and Governor table as a single sheet and revise it once a month in four minutes. Governors are reshuffled in batches; when a batch happens, update every affected page in one sitting rather than one at a time.
7. Keep a separate line for STATE SUPERLATIVES: largest producer of a crop, first state to implement a policy, state with the maximum operational SEZs, highest installed solar capacity. The superlative is always the cue in the question.
tricks: Scheme-name language identifies the state in five seconds. A Marathi name means Maharashtra, a Telugu name means Andhra Pradesh or Telangana, a Kannada name means Karnataka, a Bengali name means West Bengal, a Tamil name means Tamil Nadu, and 'Mukhyamantri ___ Yojana' in Hindi points to the Hindi belt. This is a genuine, reliable, three-option eliminator on a question you have never seen.

Honest priors for 'India's first' when you are blank: technology, industrial and financial firsts cluster in Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh; forest, tribal, wildlife and environmental firsts cluster in Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and the Northeast. Two options die honestly, which is enough to make answering worthwhile.

Big infrastructure comes with a superlative attached — longest bridge, tallest statue, largest solar park, newest airport, longest expressway. Capture the superlative and the state together, because the superlative is the cue in the stem and the state is the answer.
Read the stem for 'Lieutenant Governor'. If the question says LG or Administrator, the answer is a Union Territory, not a state — that single word eliminates every state option instantly.

Revise the CM and Governor table as one 36-row sheet rather than state by state. Four minutes a month covers what is close to a guaranteed question, and doing it as a table exposes the recent changes by contrast.

When a state item and a static geography item collide in the same question ('the Omkareshwar Floating Solar Project is in which state'), answer from the state page, not from your current-affairs memory. That is exactly why everything lives on the state page.
traps: Confusing the state that LAUNCHED a scheme with a state that later replicated or extended it. Record the launching state explicitly.
Governor versus Lieutenant Governor versus Administrator. Union Territories have LGs or Administrators; only states have Governors. Getting this wrong means answering a UT question with a state.
Assuming the CM in your notes is still in office. Date-stamp every CM and Governor entry; assembly elections and reshuffles invalidate them without warning.
Capturing the scheme's name but not its BENEFIT AMOUNT. The rupee figure per beneficiary is a standard question and it is the field most often dropped.
Ignoring Union Territories. Ladakh, Jammu & Kashmir, Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep generate news items whose answers are highly distinctive and therefore highly examinable.
Keeping state news in a date-wise diary. It cannot be revised, because no question in the history of this exam has ever asked what happened on a given date.
ga-state.timeTarget: 15 seconds per question. 'Located in which state' questions should be 10 seconds once the state pages are built.
ga-state.masteryCheck: You name the Chief Minister and the Governor of all 28 states in under eight minutes with fewer than three errors. Separately, for every 'India's first ___' item in your six-month register you name the state instantly, and for every state scheme you state the beneficiary group and the benefit amount.

ga-committees.whatItIs: Who heads which committee and on what subject — split between a permanently static list of historic banking and finance committees that every bank exam recycles, and the committees constituted inside your six-month window. 'Constituted by whom' is asked nearly as often as 'headed by whom'.
ga-committees.coreMethod:
1. Two registers, treated completely differently. (A) HISTORIC BANKING AND FINANCE COMMITTEES — static, learned once, reusable across every bank exam for the rest of your life. (B) COMMITTEES CONSTITUTED IN YOUR WINDOW — current, three-line entries.
2. Learn the static list SUBJECT-FIRST, because the subjects are distinct and memorable while the surnames blur into each other. Narasimham — banking sector reforms (two committees, 1991 and 1998). Nachiket Mor — comprehensive financial services for small businesses and low-income households. Bimal Jalan — RBI's economic capital framework. Urjit Patel — the monetary policy framework and inflation targeting. Y.H. Malegam — microfinance and later NPAs and provisioning. Damodaran — customer service in banks. P.J. Nayak — governance of bank boards. Deepak Mohanty — the medium-term path on financial inclusion. Usha Thorat — NBFCs. K.V. Kamath — the resolution framework for COVID-related stress. Nandan Nilekani — deepening digital payments. U.K. Sinha — MSMEs. Ghosh — bank frauds and malpractices. Goiporia — customer service in banks (the earlier one). N.K. Singh — the FRBM review and the 15th Finance Commission. Tarapore — capital account convertibility. Rangarajan — poverty estimation and disinvestment. Kelkar and Chelliah — tax and fiscal reforms. Swaminathan — farmers.
3. For each static entry store three fields only: Head | Subject in five words | Constituted by (RBI, the Government, or SEBI). The constituting body is a live question and also a free eliminator.
4. For committees formed in your window, add a fourth field: the report deadline. And capture the committee ON THE DAY IT IS FORMED — it gets asked in the same cycle, long before its report is published, so waiting for the report means missing the question.
5. Keep the constitutional and statutory bodies with fixed heads on the same sheet: the Finance Commission (which number and who chairs it), the Law Commission, NHRC, NCW, UPSC, CVC, CIC and the Lokpal.
6. Drill both directions in the same sitting — subject to head, and head to subject. The paper does both and you cannot predict which.
tricks: Subject-first learning is measurably more reliable than name-first, because the subjects (microfinance, NPAs, customer service, digital payments, bank board governance) are all distinct while the surnames are interchangeable under pressure. Build your recall around the subject and the name attaches to it.

The constituting body is a free eliminator you can apply with no memory at all: if the subject is monetary policy, bank governance or NBFCs, RBI constituted it. If it is taxation, fiscal policy or a Finance Commission, the Government did. If it is securities markets or investor protection, SEBI did. That reasoning alone often separates the plausible options.
Finance Commission questions always pair the NUMBER with the CHAIR. Learn the current Commission and the one before it — that pair covers almost every asking of this question.
New committees get asked in the same cycle they are announced, before any report exists. Capture on formation day, not on report day. Most aspirants do the opposite and miss the window entirely.

IBPS pads committee option sets with famous names from completely unrelated domains — a cricketer, an actor, a serving minister. If an option is a household name from outside finance, it is almost certainly a distractor.
When two committee heads share a surname, always store the initials. Storing just 'Sinha' or 'Gandhi' guarantees you a wrong answer when both appear.
traps: Narasimham Committee I versus Narasimham Committee II. Different years, different focus, and if the question names a year the number matters.
Confusing a committee with a working group, a task force, an expert group or a commission. The paper uses the exact term from the notification, and using the wrong term means you pick the wrong body.
Attributing a Government-appointed committee to the RBI, or the reverse. This is the single most common error in this topic and the constituting-body rule fixes it.
Using an outdated Finance Commission number. It changes on a fixed cycle and an old number is confidently wrong.
Learning only surnames. Store initials, always.
Waiting for a committee's report before recording the committee, and consequently missing every question asked in the intervening months.
ga-committees.masteryCheck: Given 25 committee subjects you name the head for at least 22. Given 25 heads you name the subject for at least 20. For all of them you state the constituting body correctly. Verified twice on different days, in both directions each time.
